engineeringProjects.name: ByBar Azure Integration Pipeline
engineeringProjects.summary: End-to-end Azure integration pipeline for a live Netherlands fashion brand — processing 10–20 million product records per sync with end-to-end latency under 4 seconds, fully deployed as infrastructure-as-code.
engineeringProjects.problem: A Netherlands-based fashion enterprise (ByBar) needed a reliable, high-throughput pipeline to sync 10–20 million product records into their downstream product management system — with data transformation, schema validation, and guaranteed delivery, all repeatable across environments.
engineeringProjects.context: B2B enterprise integration where data integrity and latency are business-critical. The client operates at EU enterprise scale — data volumes are large, transformation rules are complex (XSLT), and the integration must be environment-agnostic and deployable by pipeline, not manually.
engineeringProjects.myRole: Sole architect and implementer — designed the integration architecture, wrote the XSLT transformations, defined the Canonical Data Model, configured all Azure services, and deployed everything via Bicep and Azure DevOps YAML pipelines.
responsibilities: Designed end-to-end integration architecture: recurrence trigger → Logic App → XSLT transformation → Canonical Data Model → Azure Blob Storage → Azure Service Bus → downstream consumer
Wrote XSLT transformations to map source product schema to the Canonical Data Model — handling 10–20 million records per sync with structural validation
Configured and deployed Azure Logic Apps, Service Bus, Blob Storage, APIM, and Event Grid
Deployed entire integration infrastructure as code using Azure Bicep — repeatable, environment-agnostic release workflows across dev, staging, and production
Set up Azure DevOps Pipelines with YAML for automated deployment and release orchestration
engineeringProjects.architecture: Recurrence-triggered Azure Logic App ingests the product feed, passes records through an XSLT transformation layer that maps source schema to a Canonical Data Model (CDM). Transformed records are written to Azure Blob Storage for durability, then published to Azure Service Bus for ordered, guaranteed delivery to the downstream product management system. The entire infrastructure — Logic Apps, APIM, Event Grid, Service Bus — is defined in Azure Bicep and deployed via Azure DevOps YAML pipelines for environment-agnostic, repeatable releases.

decisions.title: XSLT Transformation vs. Code-Based Mapping
decisions.situation: The product records required complex structural transformation from the source schema to the Canonical Data Model. Two approaches were viable: declarative XSLT or imperative C# mapping code.
decisions.optionA: C# code-based mapping — explicit control, easier to unit test individual fields, familiar language for the team.
decisions.optionB: XSLT transformation — declarative, schema-portable, natively supported by Logic Apps without additional runtime dependencies.
decisions.rationale: XSLT integrates natively with Azure Logic Apps and is designed exactly for structured document transformation at this scale. Keeping transformation declarative and outside application code means schema changes are isolated and don't require redeployment of backend services.
decisions.tradeoff: XSLT is less familiar to most developers and harder to debug than C# code. Requires investment in XSLT tooling and understanding of XPath.
decisions.result: Transformation pipeline processes 10–20 million records per sync within the 4-second end-to-end SLA. Schema changes are applied without service redeployment.

decisions.title: Bicep IaC vs. Manual Azure Portal Configuration
decisions.situation: The integration uses 5 Azure services. The question was whether to configure them through the Azure Portal or define them entirely as Infrastructure-as-Code using Bicep.
decisions.optionA: Azure Portal configuration — faster initial setup, no Bicep learning curve, sufficient for a single environment.
decisions.optionB: Azure Bicep IaC — all services defined declaratively, version-controlled, deployable to any environment via pipeline.
decisions.rationale: An EU enterprise client requires a production-grade, auditable, repeatable deployment. Manual portal configuration creates environment drift and makes disaster recovery and staging parity impossible to guarantee.
decisions.tradeoff: Bicep adds upfront authoring time and requires understanding ARM template structure. Worth it for any multi-environment or production-grade integration.
decisions.result: Entire integration stack — Logic Apps, APIM, Event Grid, Service Bus — deployable from a single Bicep + YAML pipeline run. Zero environment drift between staging and production.

challenges: Handling 10–20 million records reliably within a 4-second SLA required careful choice of Service Bus partitioning and session handling to prevent message ordering issues at scale
XSLT transformation for deeply nested product schemas required iterative validation against real production data — source schema had undocumented edge cases that only surfaced at volume
engineeringProjects.outcome: Production integration pipeline serving a live EU enterprise client. 10–20 million product records per sync processed end-to-end in under 4 seconds. Entire infrastructure deployable via a single pipeline run — environment-agnostic, observable, repeatable.
metrics: 100% infrastructure as code via Azure Bicep
Zero-touch deployment via Azure DevOps YAML
lessonsLearned: At enterprise data volumes, choosing the right Azure primitive (Service Bus vs Storage Queue vs Event Grid) is an architecture decision with significant downstream consequences — getting it right upfront saves re-architecture later
IaC from day one is not optional on multi-environment enterprise integrations — the overhead of Bicep authoring is repaid on the first staging → production deployment

engineeringProjects.name: MyAlgoAI
engineeringProjects.summary: Production .NET C# trading platform serving 80–100 daily active users across 4 brokers — rebuilt from Node.js to Clean Architecture, API response from 10s → 300ms, full auth system designed from scratch.
engineeringProjects.problem: A production trading platform had accumulated critical technical debt: Node.js backend with monolithic data structures, no multi-threading, 10-second API response times, and an insecure legacy auth layer — all under live financial users with sub-second latency expectations.
engineeringProjects.context: Fintech production system where API latency directly affects trader response time to live market signals. The platform integrates 4 brokers and serves real-time order execution with strict uptime SLAs. Any downtime or latency spike has direct business impact.
engineeringProjects.myRole: Backend lead — architected and implemented the full rebuild from Node.js to .NET Core, owned the authentication redesign, and built the multi-threaded order execution system.
responsibilities: Architected migration from Node.js to .NET Core (C#) Clean Architecture — defined domain boundaries, application layer, and infrastructure separation
Introduced MongoDB indexing and split monolithic data structures into relational models with one-to-many relationships
Redesigned REST endpoints with async patterns and inbuilt caching
Implemented multi-threaded order execution supporting 500+ concurrent users placing orders across 4 brokers simultaneously
Designed and implemented access + refresh token architecture, RBAC, and broker-level session isolation — replacing an insecure legacy auth layer
Cut trading UI page load from 10s → 1s through React optimisation, Redux state normalisation, and broker market data caching
engineeringProjects.architecture: Clean Architecture .NET Core backend separates domain logic from infrastructure. REST endpoints use async/await with inbuilt response caching. MongoDB documents are indexed and structured with one-to-many relationships for order and broker data. Multi-threaded order execution dispatches concurrent requests across 4 broker APIs without blocking. React frontend uses WebSocket streams for real-time trade data, Redux for normalised state, and TypeScript API batching for broker market data.

decisions.title: Node.js → .NET Core: Full Rebuild vs. Incremental Refactor
decisions.situation: The Node.js backend had pervasive monolithic structure — data shapes, business logic, and infrastructure concerns deeply coupled. The question was whether to refactor incrementally or rebuild with a proper architecture.
decisions.optionA: Incremental refactor of existing Node.js — lower risk, gradual improvement, no big-bang rewrite risk.
decisions.optionB: Full rebuild in .NET Core Clean Architecture — clear domain boundaries, proper async model, type safety, and testability from the ground up.
decisions.rationale: The monolithic coupling meant any incremental refactor would carry the structural debt forward. Clean Architecture in .NET Core enabled proper separation of domain, application, and infrastructure layers — making multi-threading and caching safe to add without unintended side effects.
decisions.tradeoff: Full rebuild carries rewrite risk and requires feature parity validation against production. Mitigated by phased rollout with existing Node.js as fallback.
decisions.result: 10× throughput improvement. API response from 10s → 300ms. Platform supporting 500+ concurrent users across 4 brokers with no regression in functionality.

decisions.title: Auth Redesign: Access + Refresh Token vs. Session-Based
decisions.situation: The legacy auth layer was insecure and had no concept of broker-level session isolation — a critical risk for a multi-broker financial platform.
decisions.optionA: Server-side session store — stateful, easy to invalidate immediately, familiar pattern.
decisions.optionB: Access + refresh token architecture with RBAC and broker-level session isolation — stateless, horizontally scalable, granular authorization.
decisions.rationale: A multi-broker trading platform where different users have different broker permissions required token-level authorization claims. Broker-level session isolation is only achievable cleanly with JWTs carrying broker scope claims — sessions would require complex session-to-broker mapping.
decisions.tradeoff: Access tokens cannot be invalidated before expiry. Mitigated with short-lived access tokens (15min) and refresh token rotation with revocation on broker permission changes.
decisions.result: Clean, stateless authorization across all trading workflows. Broker-level session isolation enforced at the token claim level — no cross-broker data leakage possible.

challenges: Migrating from Node.js to .NET Core without downtime required phased rollout — running both systems in parallel during transition
Multi-threaded order execution across 4 brokers required careful thread-safety design for shared state (broker connection pools, order books)
engineeringProjects.outcome: Production trading platform with 10× throughput improvement, 97% API latency reduction (10s → 300ms), sub-second UI load, and secure multi-broker authorization. Serving 80–100 daily active users under live financial conditions.
lessonsLearned: Clean Architecture is not just a pattern preference — for a fintech system with multi-threading and multiple broker integrations, proper domain/infrastructure separation is what makes safe concurrent programming achievable

JWT broker-level session isolation must be designed before the first line of auth code is written — retrofitting broker claims onto an existing token structure is error-prone under production pressure

engineeringProjects.name: QR Dine
engineeringProjects.summary: Scalable multi-tenant SaaS for restaurant management — JWT auth, RBAC, multi-branch ordering, and high-concurrency optimisation.
engineeringProjects.problem: Restaurant chains needed a unified platform to manage QR-code-based ordering across multiple branches with separate admin and customer interfaces, secure authentication, and the ability to handle concurrent ordering load.
engineeringProjects.context: Built as an independent project to demonstrate full-stack SaaS architecture. QR Dine serves restaurant administrators and end customers across multiple branches from a single multi-tenant platform.
engineeringProjects.myRole: Sole developer — designed and built the full stack from data model through API design to frontend interfaces.
responsibilities: Designed the multi-tenant data model supporting multiple restaurant branches with isolated data
Implemented JWT-based authentication and role-based access control for admin and customer roles
Built Next.js admin interface and React client interface with shared component patterns
Optimised Node.js API and MongoDB queries for high-concurrency ordering scenarios
engineeringProjects.architecture: Multi-tenant Next.js frontend with separate admin and client surfaces shares a Node.js API layer. MongoDB stores restaurant, menu, and order data partitioned by branch. JWT tokens carry role claims (admin/customer) validated on every API route.

decisions.title: JWT + RBAC vs. Session-Based Authentication
decisions.situation: Two separate frontend apps (admin and customer) sharing a single API without shared session state.
decisions.optionA: Server-side session store — stateful, easy to invalidate, requires shared session infrastructure between frontend surfaces.
decisions.optionB: JWT with role claims — stateless, works natively across separate frontend origins without session sharing.
decisions.rationale: Two frontend apps sharing one API without a shared session store made stateless JWT the natural fit. Role claims embedded in the token meant the API could authorize any request without a session lookup.
decisions.tradeoff: JWTs cannot be invalidated before expiry. Mitigated with short expiry (15 min) and refresh token rotation.
decisions.result: Clean role-based access control across admin and customer surfaces. API authorization consistent and stateless.

challenges: Multi-tenant data isolation required careful MongoDB schema design to prevent cross-branch data leakage
engineeringProjects.outcome: Live, publicly accessible SaaS platform demonstrating full multi-tenant architecture, secure authentication, and production-ready API design.
metrics: Multi-tenant data isolation at schema level
lessonsLearned: Multi-tenant data isolation should be a schema-level constraint — moving it to application-level filter creates query complexity and security surface area

engineeringDecisions.title: Node.js → .NET Core: Full Rebuild vs. Incremental Refactor
engineeringDecisions.situation: The MyAlgoAI trading backend had deeply coupled monolithic structure in Node.js — 10-second API responses, no multi-threading, and pervasive coupling between business logic and infrastructure. The question was how to fix it.
engineeringDecisions.optionA: Incremental Node.js refactor — lower risk, gradual improvement, avoids big-bang rewrite. Tech debt addressed layer by layer.
engineeringDecisions.optionB: Full rebuild in .NET Core Clean Architecture — proper domain/application/infrastructure separation from the ground up, enabling safe multi-threading and caching.
engineeringDecisions.rationale: The monolithic coupling meant any incremental refactor would carry the structural debt forward. Multi-threaded order execution is only safe when domain logic is cleanly separated from infrastructure — something impossible to retrofit without a structural break.
engineeringDecisions.tradeoff: Full rebuild carries rewrite risk and requires feature parity validation. Mitigated by phased rollout with the existing Node.js backend as a live fallback during transition.
engineeringDecisions.result: 10× throughput improvement. API response from 10s → 300ms. Platform now handles 500+ concurrent users across 4 brokers.

engineeringDecisions.title: XSLT Transformation vs. C# Code Mapping for ByBar Pipeline
engineeringDecisions.situation: ByBar's product records required complex structural transformation from source schema to a Canonical Data Model. 10–20 million records per sync. Two approaches: declarative XSLT or imperative C# mapping code.
engineeringDecisions.optionA: C# code-based mapping — explicit control, unit-testable field by field, familiar language. Schema changes require code changes and redeployment.
engineeringDecisions.optionB: XSLT transformation — declarative, schema-portable, natively integrated in Azure Logic Apps. Schema changes are XSLT updates, not service redeployments.
engineeringDecisions.rationale: XSLT integrates natively with Azure Logic Apps at no additional runtime cost. Keeping transformation declarative and outside application code means the transformation layer can be updated independently — critical for an enterprise client where product schema evolves.
engineeringDecisions.tradeoff: XSLT is less familiar than C# and harder to debug. Requires XPath proficiency and specialist tooling for development.
engineeringDecisions.result: Transformation pipeline processes 10–20M records within the 4-second SLA. Schema updates deployed without backend service changes or downtime.

engineeringDecisions.title: Bicep IaC vs. Manual Azure Portal Configuration
engineeringDecisions.situation: ByBar integration uses 5 Azure services across multiple environments. Manual portal configuration is fast for prototyping but creates environment drift — staging and production diverge silently.
engineeringDecisions.optionA: Azure Portal configuration — faster initial setup, no Bicep authoring overhead. Acceptable for single-environment proof-of-concept.
engineeringDecisions.optionB: Azure Bicep IaC — all services version-controlled, deployable to any environment from a single pipeline run, auditable and repeatable.
engineeringDecisions.rationale: An EU enterprise client requires production-grade, auditable, repeatable deployment. Manual configuration is a maintenance liability — impossible to audit, impossible to reproduce exactly across environments, and unacceptable under enterprise SLAs.
engineeringDecisions.tradeoff: Bicep adds authoring time and requires understanding ARM template structure. This upfront cost is repaid on the first multi-environment deployment.
engineeringDecisions.result: Full integration stack deployable from a single Bicep + YAML pipeline run. Zero environment drift. Staging mirrors production exactly.

engineeringPrinciples.name: Architecture First
engineeringPrinciples.statement: Structural problems cannot be solved by adding features. Fix the architecture or carry the debt forever.
engineeringPrinciples.evidence: MyAlgoAI: Node.js → .NET Core Clean Architecture rebuild. Incremental refactor was not an option — monolithic coupling made multi-threading unsafe. Result: 10× throughput.

engineeringPrinciples.name: IaC or It Didn't Happen
engineeringPrinciples.statement: Infrastructure defined outside version control is infrastructure you cannot trust, reproduce, or audit.
engineeringPrinciples.evidence: ByBar: entire Azure integration stack (Logic Apps, APIM, Event Grid, Service Bus) defined in Bicep. Staging mirrors production exactly. Deployed by pipeline, not by hand.

engineeringPrinciples.name: Observability Is Not Optional
engineeringPrinciples.statement: A system you cannot observe is a system you cannot debug or improve. Instrument before you optimize.
engineeringPrinciples.evidence: MyAlgoAI: API latency profiling identified the specific MongoDB query patterns responsible for 10-second responses — targeted fix, not broad caching.

engineeringPrinciples.name: Design for Failure
engineeringPrinciples.statement: Network failures, token expiry, and concurrent writes are not edge cases. They are operational reality.
engineeringPrinciples.evidence: MyAlgoAI: refresh token rotation with revocation on broker permission changes. ByBar: Service Bus for guaranteed delivery — messages survive downstream consumer failures.
